absent: Full scheduler feature list and meaning of each feature bit
Callers and timing of core hold acquire and release
Complete runqueue and task structure layouts beyond fields observed here
Deadline comparison tie rules and server lifetime
Fair zero offset update rules and force idle accounting
Extension scheduler hierarchy construction and callback contracts
High resolution tick donor selection and tick handler effects
Wake queue sizing limits if any
Housekeeping mask construction and domain traversal order details

findings.text: Core scheduling offers a reference counted hold and release pair. Acquiring when the count is already nonzero only bumps the count. Acquiring from zero takes a dedicated mutex, enables the feature, then bumps the count with ordering before the increment. Releasing when more than one holder remains only decrements. Releasing the last holder schedules deferred work that disables the feature under the same mutex.

Enabling or disabling core scheduling walks every online core once while holding a CPU hotplug read guard. For each core it acquires all sibling queue locks together with interrupts saved, waits while a core wide pick is marked in flight by dropping and reacquiring, updates a per queue enabled flag for all siblings, clears a force idle start marker, then releases. Offline CPUs have only their enabled flag updated without locking. Empty tree state is asserted around the transition.

Task priority for core decisions uses a small ordered scale. Stop class is highest, then deadline service including fair tasks served by a deadline server, then realtime and deadline numeric levels, then extension class squashed to one level, then fair class squashed to a nearby lower level, then idle class lowest. Extension membership is true only when extension scheduling is enabled and the task class matches, with an alternate build where it is always false.

Pairwise ordering first compares the mapped priority with more urgent considered smaller. Equal deadline levels compare absolute deadlines from the task entity or its server entity. Equal fair levels delegate to fair ordering. Equal extension levels delegate to extension ordering when that configuration exists. All other equal levels are treated as unordered.

Core tree order is primarily by an unsigned cookie with smaller first. Ties are resolved by inverted priority so that the more urgent task sorts leftmost, using the force idle state of the local core as context. Tree search by cookie returns negative, zero or positive comparison results, and lookup plus successor walk skip tasks reported throttled for the target CPU.

Throttle state is queried through an optional class hook, defaulting to unthrottled when absent. One fair build reports throttled only when bandwidth control is in use and the task flag is set. An alternate fair build always reports unthrottled.

Extension ordering prefers a common ancestor scheduler in the hierarchy that provides a before callback, using the task schedulers when they match or the highest common ancestor otherwise. The callback is used with swapped arguments only when neither CPU is in bypass for that scheduler. Without a usable callback, a running task sorts after a waiting task, otherwise the later enqueue stamp sorts after the earlier one.

Fair ordering compares virtual runtimes after adjusting by per queue zero offsets used for force idle accounting. A positive adjusted difference means the first task sorts after the second. The arithmetic helper supports only subtraction expressed in words and fails the build for any other operator. Callers are expected to compare tasks whose queues share one core.

Acquiring two queue locks uses a global order to avoid deadlock, ordering by core identifier first when core scheduling exists and then by CPU identifier, which also keeps sibling order for flipping. After both locks are held, only skip related clock update flags are preserved on each queue while other request flags are cleared. Callers must hold interrupts disabled.

Nonblocking queue lock acquisition disables preemption to pair with the read copy update barrier used during enable. When core scheduling is disabled it attempts only the local lock. Otherwise it repeatedly samples the effective lock pointer, attempts it, and retries if the pointer changed after success or failure, reenabling preemption before returning the outcome.

Pinning a task to its queue validates that the sampled queue still matches the task CPU and that the task is not marked migrating. One form requires the task priority inheritance lock already held. The other form acquires that lock with interrupts saved. Both forms release and spin lightly while migrating is observed, then retry until stable, returning with the queue pinned.

High resolution tick programming defers work requested inside schedule. Entering schedule records deferred mode and captures any pending timer rearm request. Starting a slice during deferral only records start intent plus delay. Exiting applies a pending start by computing a new expiry and conditionally restarting, cancels a queued timer when going idle with no pending start, performs any captured rearm, then returns to idle mode.

The per queue high resolution timer callback runs on the queue CPU, locks the queue, refreshes its clock, invokes the donor task tick handler for one tick, unlocks, and requests no restart. Restart decisions treat an unqueued or currently running timer as needing restart, otherwise only when the new expiry differs substantially from the queued expiry.

High resolution tick start programs the local timer directly but uses an asynchronous cross call for a remote queue. Queue initialization sets up that cross call plus timer in one build and does nothing in an alternate build. Clearing, entering schedule and exiting schedule likewise have active variants and empty variants selected by configuration.

Core scheduling state observed on queues includes a shared tree of tasks, a boolean enabled flag per queue, a shared core control with CPU identity, force idle nesting count and start marker, plus an in flight guard for core wide picks. Task state observed includes an unsigned cookie, a tree node, a deadline server pointer, class pointer, numeric priority, on CPU flag, and extension enqueue stamp.

Deferred wakeups use a head with first node and tail link pointer plus an intrusive node per task. Insertion links at the tail only if the node was previously unlinked, using a relaxed compare exchange after a write barrier. Draining walks from first to tail marker, clears each node link with ordered store, wakes the owner, and drops the extra reference, allowing immediate reinsertion.

Public wake helpers add a task to a local deferred queue while holding an extra task reference on success, with a safe variant that drops a caller held reference when insertion is redundant. A drain helper wakes each queued task in order. Direct process wakeup requests a normal state wake with no mode flags.

Marking need reschedule for a polling task first checks a polling flag and returns false when absent, returns true early if reschedule already pending, otherwise attempts to set the reschedule flag with a compare exchange loop. An alternate build always reports false and never touches flags.

Lazy preemption selects a lazy reschedule flag when a dynamic static key or a compile time option enables lazy mode, otherwise the regular reschedule flag. A lazy reschedule helper applies that selection to a queue. A remote CPU helper locks the target queue with interrupts saved and requests reschedule only when the CPU is online or is the caller.

Timer target selection prefers the caller when it allows kernel noise and is busy, remembering it as fallback when idle. Otherwise it scans scheduler domains outward for another allowed busy CPU, skipping the caller. If none is busy it falls back to the remembered caller or to any allowed CPU.
A topology helper reports the last level cache identifier for the CPU where a task currently resides. Two trace helpers record current state changes and need reschedule events with CPU identity.

Scheduler features are held as a mostly read bitmask assembled from an included feature list plus zero terminator. Core enable, paravirtual steal queue enable, and lazy preemption use static branch keys defaulting to disabled, with lazy mode also having a compile time selected alternate.

Flipping core mode while a core wide pick holds dropped locks would rebind the effective lock pointer underneath it, so the flip path waits for the in flight marker to clear. Trees must be empty across all possible CPUs before either direction of the transition, enforced by warnings.

Queue identity can change concurrently due to migration and core mode flips can change the effective lock, so all acquisition paths revalidate the sampled queue and lock pointer after locking and retry or spin while a migrating marker is present. Missing the retry would lock the wrong queue or miss a wakeup.

Concurrent deferred wake insertions for the same task must result in a single queue entry, so insertion uses an atomic claim and callers manage references accordingly. Draining must clear the link before waking so the task can be requeued immediately without losing a later wakeup.

Core scheduling lifecycle has disabled with zero holders and enabled with at least one holder. The first acquisition moves from disabled to enabled under mutex. The last release does not disable inline but defers disable to system work context, coalescing repeated last releases through pending work state.
High resolution tick scheduler mode none is zero, defer uses the second bit, start uses the third bit, rearm uses the fourth bit.

Mapped core priorities are negative two for stop, negative one for deadline service, numeric realtime range for realtime and deadline, one hundred nineteen for fair squash, one hundred twenty for extension squash, and one hundred forty for idle.

Reschedule latency warning threshold defaults to one hundred milliseconds with single shot warnings enabled by default. Migration batch break uses a build defined migrate break constant. A global integer records whether the scheduler is running.

Programmed slices are clamped to a minimum of ten thousand nanoseconds to avoid timer overload. A queued timer is considered needing rearm only when the absolute expiry shift exceeds five thousand nanoseconds.

Two task extension callbacks temporarily publish both task pointers in dedicated current task slots with a warning if the first slot was already occupied, invoke the underlying operation, then clear both slots. Bypass state is read from per CPU scheduler flags masked for bypass with an unlikely hint.
A queue counts as idle only when its current task is its idle task and both its running count and its pending wake count are zero.
